doc.title: Billy Bauer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Tone elements, traditionalists, and not hurting other players
summary: The four elements of a tone; he calls himself no traditionalist and says his gift is blending without crowding other players, as Louis Armstrong's sidemen did.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: So I say what are they? They don’t know. I say what’s a musical tone? I don’t want to embarrass you.
Yeah. A note represents a musical tone.
All right. Well a tone has pitch.
And it has — oh boy — inflection?
Well timbre. It’s the sound, the sound.

Yeah. It could be two instruments — well it could be the same instrument and you’ve got to get your sound to come out. That’s why you know like if I take a guitar player, you know, and I’ve got a French guy, he come over from France. And he’s a Django Reinhardt, he thinks he’s a Django Reinhardt. I says well that’s all right but you’re a traditionalist. So don’t forget, I told you you’re a traditionalist. I says a lot of the guys playing Dixieland, you know, they play Dixieland music. I say I’m not a traditionalist. I don’t care what you play. If you want to play you play. But a traditionalist would be somebody who’s staying like Dixieland or Django Reinhardt, like 50 years ago. But I seem to go from — wherever I go I seem to get in with other guys and I guess I’ve got some kind of a thing that I blend with them in some sort. I don’t hurt their playing. And that’s a big deal, I try to tell them.
That’s an important phrase right there. Don’t hurt their playing.

Oh well sure. That’s right. That’s why you might not play so good, but they play good. And I think Louis Armstrong, when I listen to Louis Armstrong, some of his early bands, I’d say gee why is he having a saxophone player, that guy, he don’t play that good you know. But now I realize that Louis could play good with these guys. You know, like if you get with some good players, sometimes they sound good but you feel them crowding you out.
